analysis.one_liner: Strengthens enforcement of equal-pay laws for women, including banning salary-history questions and punishing pay secrecy rules.
analysis.headline: The bill had 48 cosponsors — nearly half the Senate, all of them Democrats or Independents — but never received a committee markup, hearing, or floor vote before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The Paycheck Fairness Act would strengthen the Equal Pay Act of 1963, which bans paying women less than men for the same work. It would narrow the excuses employers can use to justify pay gaps, add damages and class-action rights for workers who sue, outlaw contracts and rules that stop employees from discussing their wages, and prohibit employers from using a job applicant's past salary to set her new pay. It would also require employers to report pay data broken down by sex and race so the government can spot discrimination patterns.
analysis.who_benefits: Women workers who are paid less than male colleagues for the same work. Stronger enforcement means they could recover real damages instead of only back pay, sue as a class, and challenge excuses like 'negotiation skill' when a cheaper alternative practice exists. All workers gain the legal right to discuss and disclose their own wages without retaliation, and job applicants no longer have a previous employer's low pay carried forward to cap their next salary. The bill also funds negotiation-skills training for girls and women and requires federal data collection on pay by sex, race, and national origin to help spot discrimination.

how_it_helps.text: It narrows the defense employers can use in equal-pay cases: a pay gap based on education, training, or experience is only allowed if it is job-related, consistent with business necessity, accounts for the entire gap, and the employer has not refused a reasonable alternative that would avoid the gap.

It makes it unlawful to require an employee to sign a contract or waiver prohibiting the employee from disclosing information about the employee's wages, and strengthens protections against retaliation for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages.

It adds compensatory and, for malicious or reckless violations, punitive damages — with expert fees recoverable — and allows equal-pay cases to be maintained as class actions under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.

It makes it an unlawful practice for an employer to rely on or seek a prospective employee's wage history, with civil penalties of $5,000 for a first offense and up to $10,000 in special damages per affected person, except that prior wages may be used only to support a higher offer after an offer is made.

It directs the EEOC to issue regulations requiring employers to report compensation, hiring, termination, and promotion data disaggregated by sex, race, and national origin, to support enforcement of pay-discrimination laws.

It authorizes $15 million, including a Department of Labor grant program for negotiation-skills training for girls and women, and directs studies and public information on eliminating pay disparities.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, chiefly larger ones (small businesses are exempt to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act). They would face expanded litigation exposure including class actions and punitive damages, a narrowed set of defenses in equal-pay lawsuits, new federal pay-data reporting, penalties for asking about salary history, and the end of pay-secrecy practices that keep wage disparities invisible. Federal contractors would face broader compensation-data surveys and investigations.

drawbacks.text: The bill would significantly raise the cost and risk of employment litigation. By allowing class actions, compensatory and punitive damages, and expert fees, and by narrowing the business-necessity defense, it exposes employers to larger judgments for pay practices that may reflect neutral factors, and it places the burden on employers to prove their pay differences are justified.

The prohibition on seeking or relying on a candidate's wage history, even voluntarily until after an offer is made, removes information many employers use to calibrate offers, and the ban on contracts restricting wage disclosure overrides confidentiality arrangements some employers and employees have agreed to.

The bill directs new data collection by the EEOC and the Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs, adding reporting burdens that the bill itself acknowledges must be weighed against enforcement value.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside is direct and substantial: real damages instead of token ones, the ability to sue as a group, the right to talk about pay, and the removal of a practice that lets past discrimination follow a woman from job to job. The costs fall mainly on employers in the form of reporting, compliance, and litigation exposure, and some of that exposure would attach to legitimate pay factors before an employer has documented them. The bill includes accommodations — a small-business exemption, technical-assistance materials, a six-month phase-in, and a requirement that regulators weigh reporting burdens — but it is unambiguously a bill that shifts power and money toward employees in pay-discrimination disputes.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act in the Senate on April 4, 2017, joined by 42 other Democratic senators as original sponsors.
The bill gathered 48 cosponsors — 47 Democrats and 1 Independent — meaning roughly half the Senate supported it, with no Republican cosponsors.
After being read twice, it was referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced.
The action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote — before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, particularly large ones and federal contractors, are better off because the bill died: they face no expanded equal-pay liability, no class-action exposure, no new pay-data reporting requirements, and no restriction on using salary history in hiring. Women workers who would have gained stronger remedies receive nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have faced new liability

sides.party_line_note: All 48 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent who caucuses with Democrats, with no Republican support, and the committee that buried the bill was chaired by a Republican in a Senate where Republicans held the majority.

industries.note: The bill would have expanded their litigation exposure in equal-pay cases — compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, expert fees — and narrowed the defenses they can raise. Its defeat leaves in place pay-secrecy practices and salary-history reliance that keep pay disparities from being challenged.

The bill would have directed the contract-compliance office to use broader investigative methods and to survey compensation data at least annually at half of nonconstruction contractor establishments for enforcement purposes. Its defeat preserves the lighter-touch enforcement regime for contractors.

The bill exempts small businesses to the same extent they are exempt from the Fair Labor Standards Act, and provides technical assistance materials for compliance, so most small employers would have avoided its requirements entirely.

Salary-history bans and new pay-data reporting would have changed hiring workflows and generated compliance work; firms in this space would have gained business from the changes while their clients absorbed the cost.
